edges.effect_quant: Across non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes trials, SMBG shows a modest short-term HbA1c benefit that tends to fade over time. A 2018 meta-analysis found reductions of -0.31% at 12 weeks and -0.34% at 24 weeks, while an individual-patient-data meta-analysis found an average six-month benefit of about 0.25% HbA1c.
edges.population: adults with type 2 diabetes not treated with insulin or intensive insulin regimens
edges.mechanism: Self-monitoring of blood glucose may help some patients link food, medication, and lifestyle patterns to glucose excursions, which can support earlier behavior or medication adjustment. The effect is often limited when monitoring is not paired with clear education or actionable treatment changes.
edges.summary: The evidence supports a small short-term HbA1c improvement from SMBG in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, but the effect is inconsistent and often not sustained long term. That makes this a mixed but real self-management tool rather than a universally effective glycemic intervention.
edges.caveats: Benefits appear larger in patients with poorer baseline glycemic control and in shorter follow-up windows. Several trials found little or no durable HbA1c advantage at one year, and SMBG can add burden without much gain when the results are not used to change treatment or behavior.

evidence.notes: Meta-analysis of individual patient data in randomised trials of self monitoring of blood glucose in people with non-insulin treated type 2 diabetes.

evidence.citation: Malanda UL et al 2012 Cochrane Database Syst Rev
evidence.notes: Self-monitoring of blood glucose in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus who are not using insulin.
